title: Introduction to Machine Learning in Design & Infrastructure
text: print the 12-row dataset extracts (one per team), the Problem Hunt board sheets, the paper laptop-access survey and the question card for the challenge. Open by saying how long you have been doing this and one thing you got wrong recently. A room of beginners needs to know the lecturer is fallible before it will risk being wrong out loud.

title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
text: read these out. Students at zero need to know the session has a bottom — that it is finite and achievable — or the volume of new words feels limitless. Come back to this slide at the end and ask them to self-assess against it: ninety seconds, and the cheapest way to make a three-hour session feel like progress.

title: HOW TODAY RUNS
text: put this up and leave it up while you explain. Say the break time out loud so nobody spends the first hour wondering.

title: THE SEMESTER
text: say the no-memorisation point plainly. If you are teaching a Friday cohort, flag now that Friday 9 October is Independence Day and Week 5 will be delivered as a recorded package.

title: THE PROMISE
text: two minutes on this — it is the motivation slide of the session. Name the utterance you want to kill, 'Sir, what should I type?', and the one you want by December: 'we tried three approaches, the first two failed because of X, so we are testing the third.'

title: SEGMENT 1
text: keep to time. The temptation is to spend forty minutes on admin; do not. The hands-on prediction exercise is what makes them come back next week.

title: What I expect, and what you can expect back
text: read the 'ask well' item slowly. It is the single behaviour that most changes what a beginner gets from the semester.

title: SEGMENT 2
text: this segment is new and it is worth protecting. Tell them explicitly that the structure is not a syllabus you invented.

title: THE TERRITORY
text: walk it in order, about seventy seconds per column. Do not explain the individual terms. Say plainly that nobody expects them to know what a transformer is today.

title: WHERE YOU ALREADY ARE
text: this slide exists to counter the belief that machine learning belongs to computer scientists. Say directly that the hard prerequisite for the field is the mathematics and they have already done it. Watch the room change posture.

title: WHERE IT LEADS
text: expect the question 'what job does this get me?'. Answer it here rather than deflecting it to later in the semester.

title: SEGMENT 3
text: keep it tight and move to the real work in the block on rules and learning.

title: The words, and how they nest
text: draw this on the board as well as showing it. Drawn beats projected for a nested diagram.

title: DEFINITION
text: write the definition on the board and leave it there for the whole session.

title: DEFINITION
text: expect pushback here — they want the models. Give the eighty-twenty split honestly and move on.

title: SEGMENT 4
text: if you are running out of time elsewhere, protect this segment.

title: THE QUESTION THIS COURSE STARTS FROM
text: ask the room how they would answer it today, then do not resolve it. The paper exercise resolves it.

title: THE ACTUAL IDEA
text: walk the two columns slowly, left then right, then give the domain example. If a student asks which is better, ask them for a problem where they know the rule and one where they do not.

title: When to write the rule, and when to learn it from data
text: say out loud that most of engineering stays in the left-hand column. It protects you from the charge of selling a technique.

title: THE VOCABULARY
text: five minutes here at least. Point at the table and ask individual students 'feature or target?' four or five times until the answers come back quickly, then put the harder question about targets becoming features.

title: DEFINITION
text: plant the causation point in one sentence and do not develop it here.

title: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
text: ninety seconds in pairs before you reveal, and do not take an answer aloud immediately. Accept any answer to B that notices the timing problem.

title: How did you do?
text: write 'data leakage' on the board and tell them it will come back in Week 10.

title: SEGMENT 5
text: form teams HERE and keep them all semester. Mix by ability rather than friendship — use the Week 1 survey if you have it, otherwise count off around the room. Hand out the printed 12-row extracts now, one per team, plus a blank sheet.

title: TEAM TASK · 15 MINUTES
text: circulate and ask 'why that number?' Do not help. If a team is stuck, ask which column they think matters most. Some teams will average everything and some will spot the trend; you contrast the two afterwards.

title: WORKED EXAMPLE
text: show this AFTER they have tried, never before. Handing them the method first destroys the exercise.

title: THE REVEAL
text: collect every team's number on the board before revealing. Then reveal, ask the closest team to explain their method, and ask whether that method would still be best on a different case. Usually nobody knows, and that is the honest answer.

title: NAMING IT
text: go slowly here. This is the pedagogical payoff of the whole session.

title: 10 minutes
text: take the break. Do not skip it to catch up — attention at ninety minutes is genuinely gone and the challenge segment needs them fresh.

title: DEFINITION
text: drill it. Call out five problems from their discipline and have the room answer 'number' or 'category' in unison. Thirty seconds, and it sticks far better than the definition.

title: SEGMENT 7
text: this segment buys credibility for the whole semester. Engineering students are rightly sceptical of hype, and showing the limits early earns the right to teach the rest.

title: THE LIMITS
text: say the caption twice. Ask the room for a case from their own experience that hits limit one — somebody always has a story about records that were never kept.

title: MADE CONCRETE
text: read each of the four out and then ask for one more example from the room; their examples are better than yours because they own them. The closing paragraph is the project gate, so say it now and Week 9 will not be a surprise.

title: SEGMENT 8
text: say out loud that you will not answer questions in this segment, and why. Carry the printed question card — it is there to stop YOU giving answers, which is harder than it sounds.

title: CHALLENGE
text: seed prompts, only if a team is genuinely stuck: Concrete strength from a mix design, without waiting 28 days · A building's energy use before it is built · Which sections of road will deteriorate first · Defect severity from inspection records, more consistently than three inspectors. Harvest every board onto a class list afterwards — students take their own idea far more seriously than one you hand them.

title: How your team works, all semester
text: collect the charters — you need the team list for the Week 9 project registration anyway. The charter takes five minutes and prevents most of the free-riding complaints that otherwise arrive in Week 12.

title: ASSIGNMENT
text: collect the paper laptop-access survey before they leave. Paper gets a 100 per cent return; a form does not.

text: link verified as existing on 7 September 2026. The runtime was not stated in the source, so check it and write it on the slide before you issue the deck.

title: SEGMENT 10
text: tell them explicitly that the deck continues past the end of the session. Students do not read past the last slide you present unless told to.

title: MODULE SUMMARY
text: come back to the learning objectives slide after this and ask for a show of hands against each. Ninety seconds, and it converts a long session into visible progress.

title: GLOSSARY — KEEP THIS SLIDE
text: do not teach the last two entries today.

text: open the Form, project the QR, and give it exactly five minutes. Afterwards look at the responses-by-question view — any question most of the room got wrong is next week's five-minute reteach.

title: THE ONE THING TO REMEMBER
text: close on the promise you opened with, then repeat the four practical instructions. Stay behind for ten minutes — the students who need the most help will not ask in front of the room.
